Fluid mechanics

 Home Physics Branches of physics
OurBigBook.com Words: 136k Articles: 2k
Fluid mechanics studies the motion and forces of liquids and gases. Its central simplification is the continuum approximation: replace individual molecules by bulk properties defined at every position and time. The averaging region must contain many molecules while remaining small compared with the distances over which those properties vary. A fluid element is such a small material parcel, rather than a single molecule. This connects fluid mechanics to continuum mechanics and makes calculus useful for describing flow. [ref]
Three basic fields are the velocity field u(x,t), the mass density ρ(x,t) and the pressure p(x,t). The first gives a parcel's instantaneous velocity; the second gives mass per unit volume. The pressure contributes an inward normal traction −pn across a surface with outward unit normal n. Thus pressure is a stress, measured in Pa=Nm−2, and may vary with position even in incompressible flow. Additional viscous stresses can act tangentially. [ref]
The guiding questions are what must be conserved and which forces matter. Mass conservation constrains the velocity field; momentum conservation determines its response to pressure gradients, viscosity and body forces. An incompressible flow model, a Reynolds number estimate and Bernoulli's principle answer different parts of a problem. Their appeal is that a few carefully stated assumptions can determine useful quantities before the entire velocity field is known.

Wall slip

Words: 28
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Relative tangential motion between material and its solid boundary. In rheometry it can produce an apparent shear rate greater than the actual bulk rate and distort inferred viscosity or modulus.

Focal length of a rotating liquid mirror

Words: 33
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A liquid in steady rigid rotation has a free surface z−z0​=Ω2r2/(2g). Comparing with a paraboloid z−z0​=r2/(4f) gives f=g/(2Ω2). The result follows from hydrostatic equilibrium in the rotating frame and is independent of density.

Pump

Words: 96 Articles: 2
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A device that supplies mechanical energy to a fluid to drive a flow. A specified pump installation does not by itself determine the resulting mass flow rate; the connected system's resistance also matters.

Centrifugal pump

Words: 65 Articles: 1
Pump OurBigBook.com
A rotating-impeller pump that transfers mechanical energy to a fluid. At a fixed speed its head varies with flow; its characteristic curve and the connected system determine the pump operating point.

Pump operating point

Words: 37
Centrifugal pump OurBigBook.com
The flow and head at which a pump's characteristic curve intersects the hydraulic system's required-head curve. Increasing system resistance at unchanged speed normally reduces flow on a conventional falling pump curve.[ref]

Hydraulic diameter (Dh​=4A/Pw​)

Words: 29
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Four times a flow passage's cross-sectional area divided by its wetted perimeter. It provides a characteristic length for many internal-flow correlations, with applicability depending on geometry and flow regime.

Computational fluid dynamics

Words: 18
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Numerical solution of fluid-flow models. In fossil functional analysis, reconstructed geometry, material assumptions and boundary conditions constrain the interpretation.

Microfluidics

Words: 393 Articles: 5
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Microfluidics controls and studies small fluid volumes in confined channels. In cellular assays it can impose reproducible flow and chemical fields, but channel geometry, wall interactions and flow-induced stresses can themselves alter behaviour.

Nanopore

Words: 242 Articles: 2
Microfluidics OurBigBook.com
A nanopore is a channel or aperture with a nanometre-scale constriction. A solid-state realization can connect conducting liquid reservoirs, permitting ionic current to report particle passage through resistive-pulse sensing. A geometrical pore diameter alone does not determine its conductance: axial shape, reservoir access, surface charge, solution conductivity and interfacial effects can all matter. This definition concerns a physical aperture, without a biological application.

Ionic resistance of a conical pore (R=ρL/(πab))

Words: 181 Articles: 1
Nanopore OurBigBook.com
In a one-dimensional Ohmic approximation, a linear conical frustum of length L, end radii a,b>0 and ionic resistivity ρ has r(z)=a+(b−a)z/L. Conservation of electric current gives dR=ρdz/[πr(z)2]. Integration yields the displayed resistance. Two identical opposed frusta, each of length l, have resistance 2ρl/(πab), whether their central junction is the wider or narrower end. Their local field profiles nevertheless differ. The approximation neglects surface conduction and resistance outside the defined pore, and is not an exact three-dimensional field solution for arbitrary wall slope.
Electrophoretic transit time in a conical pore (t=∫dz/[μE(z)])
Words: 95
Ionic resistance of a conical pore OurBigBook.com
For a point-like object with constant electrophoretic mobility, deterministic traversal is the integral of inverse local drift speed. In a conical frustum of length L at pore voltage V, the one-dimensional field is E(z)=Vab/[Lr(z)2]. Integrating gives t=L2(b/a+1+a/b)/(3μV) for positive μV. For two symmetric frusta of total length 2l and the same total pore voltage, replace L by 2l. The inequality b/a+a/b≥2 shows that this nonuniform field cannot produce a shorter deterministic point-particle transit than a uniform field at fixed total length and voltage. Reservoir forces, diffusion, adsorption and finite-object conformation are additional physics.

Resistive-pulse sensing

Words: 119 Articles: 1
Microfluidics OurBigBook.com
Electrical detection of particles passing through a conducting-liquid aperture. A particle changes the effective pore conductance transiently; pulse amplitude and duration depend on geometry, transport and interfacial charge, so calibration is essential.

Position-dependent resistive pulse (ΔR(z)∝ρΩ/A(z)2)

Words: 87
Resistive-pulse sensing OurBigBook.com
A small insulating object of excluded volume Ω perturbs an Ohmic pore most strongly where the pore cross-sectional area A is small. In a local weak-blockage model, replacing a small conducting volume gives the displayed resistance scaling, with a shape-dependent coefficient. At fixed voltage, ΔI≃−I0​ΔR/R0​. A symmetric pore with narrow ends and a wide middle can therefore resolve two end features in a passage pulse. This is a conditional volume-exclusion model: charged-particle ion transport, surface interactions and bandwidth can change the observed sign, amplitude and shape.

Magnus effect

Words: 66
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
The Magnus effect is a transverse force on a spinning body in relative motion through a fluid. Rotation changes the surrounding circulation, pressure distribution and wake. In a two-dimensional cylinder model, the Kutta–Joukowski theorem gives force per unit span F′=ρU×(Γz^), with relative fluid velocity U and circulation Γ positive anticlockwise viewed from +z. Real viscosity and boundary-layer behavior help determine the circulation; impermeability alone does not determine it from spin rate.

Laminar flow

Words: 1k Articles: 1
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Laminar flow is a regime of fluid flow in which the motion remains organized, with neighboring fluid parcels following smooth, coherent paths rather than the irregular interacting fluctuations characteristic of turbulence. In a straight pipe, the simplest example consists of coaxial layers sliding past one another. This describes the character of the motion, not a requirement that every parcel have the same velocity. Nor does it require steady flow: a smooth profile can evolve in time as viscosity transmits motion from a newly moving wall into a resting fluid. The unsteady wall-driven solution provides an explicit example. [ref]
The Reynolds pipe-and-dye experiment makes this distinction visible. A thin injected dye band can remain coherent in laminar flow, whereas irregular motion can fold it and carry dye across the pipe. However, molecular diffusion can spread dye even in laminar flow, and an inlet disturbance can move a coherent band without producing turbulence. A dye band is a streakline, not a measurement of the entire velocity field; in steady flow an ideal passive tracer's streakline coincides with a streamline. Reynolds explicitly distinguished a wandering band from one broken into eddies. [ref]
For a circular pipe of internal diameter D, define the mean axial velocity U using the volumetric flow rate Q and cross-sectional area A:
A=4πD2​,U=AQ​,ReD​=νUD​=μρUD​=πDν4Q​.
(1)
Here ρ is mass density, μ is dynamic viscosity and ν=μ/ρ is kinematic viscosity. This particular Reynolds number uses the diameter and mean velocity, not the radius or centreline velocity. Small Reynolds number generally favors laminar flow, but a single universal critical Reynolds number does not distinguish it from turbulence in all geometries and experiments. Even in a given pipe, inlet conditions and the magnitude of disturbances affect the observed onset. Reynolds demonstrated this dependence by deliberately inserting a wire coil. [ref]
The quantitative example above assumes steady flow, incompressible flow, a Newtonian fluid with constant dynamic viscosity, a straight horizontal circular pipe of radius R=D/2, stationary walls satisfying the no-slip boundary condition, and fully developed flow. The last assumption means that the axial velocity profile no longer changes downstream. A positive pressure drop Δp=pin​−pout​ over a developed length L gives the Hagen-Poiseuille equation:
u(r)=4μLΔp​(R2−r2)=2U(1−R2r2​),Q=∫0R​u(r)2πrdr=8μLπR4Δp​.
(2)
The velocity is zero at the wall and maximal at the centre. Averaging over the circular area, whose annuli have area 2πrdr, gives U=u(0)/2; averaging along one diameter would give a different answer. These assumptions produce a parabola, rather than every laminar flow having a parabolic profile. [ref]
As a stipulated calculation, take D=0.010m, U=0.10ms−1, ρ=1000kgm−3, μ=0.0010Pas and L=1.0m, and assume the developed laminar flow above. Then ν=10−6m2s−1, ReD​=1000, u(0)=0.20ms−1, Q=7.85×10−6m3s−1 (about 0.471Lmin−1), and Δp=32μLU/D2=32Pa. These are predictions from chosen parameters, not measurements or a claim that ReD​=1000 guarantees laminar flow in every apparatus.
The beauty of this example is that a spatially varying velocity field still gives an exact relation between two accessible measurements, pressure drop and volumetric flow rate. It predicts the hydraulic resistance Δp/Q=8μL/(πR4). Doubling the radius therefore multiplies Q by sixteen at fixed pressure drop, length and dynamic viscosity, provided the model remains applicable. This makes the laminar flow model useful for sizing narrow tubes or determining dynamic viscosity. It also explains why a persistent narrow dye band can be informative without implying that the fluid is moving as a uniform plug.

Reynolds pipe-and-dye experiment

Words: 732
Laminar flow OurBigBook.com
In his 1883 paper, Osborne Reynolds investigated how the character of pipe flow depends jointly on velocity, pipe diameter and viscosity. His final dye apparatus drew water from a large glass tank through a horizontal glass tube with a smooth trumpet-shaped entrance. A separate reservoir supplied strongly colored water just upstream of the entrance; a valve below the tank controlled the outflow. The glass tube was immersed in the tank, so its internal dye band could be watched. Reynolds repeated the trials with different tube diameters and water temperatures. [ref]
The volumetric flow rate was measured independently of the appearance of the dye. Reynolds timed a one-inch fall of the tank's water level, corresponding to a calibrated discharged volume. In modern notation, if this volume is V and the elapsed time is Δt, then Q=V/Δt and U=4V/(πD2Δt). He determined the glass tubes' internal diameters by filling them with water. For a uniform bore, a known filled length ℓ and measured water volume Vtube​ determine D=4Vtube​/(πℓ)​; checking bore uniformity matters because the same volume would only give an average cross-section in a tapered tube. Thermometers at different tank levels checked both the temperature and its uniformity. Reynolds compared the viscosity at different temperatures using Poiseuille's results and checked his own water by separate experiments of that type. Thus the Reynolds number estimate did not come from judging the dye band or from assuming that transition occurred at a preset value. [ref]
A practical repetition can instead collect a known outflow volume in a measuring vessel and time its collection, or weigh the collected water and divide its mass by mass density. Measure the internal diameter, rather than the external diameter, and obtain kinematic viscosity at the measured water temperature from independently established properties or a separate viscosity measurement. Record the dye appearance and observation position alongside Q, D, temperature and the resulting Reynolds number. These are alternative measurement procedures following Q=V/Δt, not additional historical claims about Reynolds' dye apparatus.
Begin with settled water and a small dye supply, then open the outlet valve in small steps. Reynolds saw a thin straight band at sufficiently low speeds. With a tank that had not fully settled, the band could wander while retaining its coherence. At higher discharge it could abruptly spread into the surrounding water downstream of the entrance. Short illumination by an electric spark resolved curls within what otherwise looked like a colored cloud. This connected the visible breakup with internal irregular motion rather than merely the appearance of an opaque pipe. [ref]
The controls are part of the result. Reynolds used a smooth entrance and let the tank rest to reduce inlet disturbances. He found that a heated tank could retain slow circulation as it cooled, so measuring one temperature was insufficient: thermal uniformity and residual motion also mattered. His wire-coil trial broke up the band below the previous onset speed, but he explicitly cautioned that once the dye was mixed he could not tell from that dye alone whether the motion became orderly again farther along the tube. In a repetition, keep the dye supply small enough to act approximately as a passive scalar, avoid a strong injection jet, and record the inlet condition and downstream observation distance. If also testing the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, allow the profile to develop and measure pressure drop between positions within the developed region; do not treat the entrance and outlet losses as part of its uniform pressure gradient. The dye experiment by itself does not establish fully developed flow. [ref]
The experiment's usefulness is that it compares a visible change in the motion with independently measured scales. Repeating it with several diameters and temperatures, while controlling disturbances, tests the organizing role of the Reynolds number. Its limitations are equally instructive: dye is a tracer of transport, diffusion still acts in laminar flow, and a local dye observation cannot by itself prove that turbulence persists throughout an arbitrarily long pipe.

The reference connection determines which pressure difference is being measured.

U-tube differential manometer (Δp=pL​−pR​=ρg(zR​−zL​))

Words: 990 Articles: 2
Manometer OurBigBook.com
A U-tube differential manometer contains a connected column of liquid with one gas connection above each liquid meniscus. Write pL​,pR​ for the left and right pressures, and zL​,zR​ for the meniscus heights on an upward vertical coordinate. Assume constant mass density ρ and downward gravitational acceleration of magnitude g; neglect the gas column's mass density and differences in capillary pressure. The signed vertical length difference Δh=zR​−zL​ then gives
Δp=pL​−pR​=ρgΔh.
(3)
Larger left pressure means a lower left liquid meniscus: pL​>pR​ implies zL​<zR​. Equal pressures give equal meniscus heights.
The balance follows directly from hydrostatic pressure. At a common height z0​ below both surfaces, the two points in the connected homogeneous liquid have equal pressure:
pL​+ρg(zL​−z0​)=pR​+ρg(zR​−z0​).
(4)
Subtracting cancels the common bottom depth and leaves pL​−pR​=ρg(zR​−zL​). The same-height rule follows from hydrostatic equilibrium, ∇p=−ρgez​: a horizontal displacement changes no pressure, and for constant ρ the quantity p+ρgz is constant throughout the connected liquid. Equal height alone is insufficient for unrelated vessels or for fluid flow with significant acceleration.
For an original constructed example, choose water of stipulated mass density ρ=1000kgm−3, gravitational acceleration g=9.81ms−2, and vertical length difference Δh=0.060m. Then
Δp=1000×9.81×0.060=588.6Pa.
(5)
The SI pressure unit is the pascal: the product has units kgm−3×ms−2×m=kgm−1s−2=Pa. Swapping the two connections gives −588.6Pa and reverses which liquid meniscus is lower. In equal-bore arms, volume conservation makes each surface move 30mm from its initial equal-height position; using only one surface's displacement would halve the inferred pressure. With unequal arm areas AL​,AR​, a left fall a and right rise b instead obey AL​a=AR​b, while the vertical length difference is still a+b.
If the right port is open to the local atmosphere, pL​−pR​ is the left gauge pressure. Only with that reference and known atmospheric pressure can one obtain absolute pressure from
pL,abs​=patmosphere​+pL,gauge​.
(6)
For an explicitly stipulated atmospheric pressure of 100000Pa, the example gives 100588.6Pa absolute pressure. If the right port is connected to another vessel or a pressure tapping, the same reading is a differential pressure and supplies no absolute pressure without knowing that reference.[ref]

Manometer height-to-pressure calibration (d(Δp)/d(Δh)=ρg)

Words: 298
U-tube differential manometer OurBigBook.com
The ideal measurement calibration is a straight line through the equal-pressure zero. For the stipulated water mass density and gravitational acceleration above, its slope is 9.81Pa per vertical millimetre. A lower liquid mass density gives a larger length change for the same pressure, improving the height-reading contribution to measurement resolution but requiring more vertical space for a given pressure range. The pressure scale depends on the actual mass density, which depends on temperature; 1000kgm−3 here is a chosen model value, not an exact property of all water samples.
Suppose each liquid meniscus height is rounded to the nearest scale division q=1mm. Each height measurement error lies within q/2, so the error in their difference lies within q. The resulting pressure error is bounded by ρgq=9.81Pa. To quantify a standard uncertainty, make the additional model assumption that the two rounding errors are independent random variables, each having a continuous uniform distribution on [−q/2,q/2]. Each then has variance q2/12; adding the two variances gives
u(Δh)=6​q​,u(Δp)=6​ρgq​=4.0049Pa.
(7)
Here u denotes standard uncertainty. The 9.81Pa worst-case bound and 4.0049Pa standard uncertainty answer different questions. At 588.6Pa they are respectively 1.67% and 0.680% of the reading. Shared reading bias or a different reading method can violate the assumed independence.
If the mass density, gravitational acceleration and height difference also have small independent standard uncertainties, a first-order estimate follows from the partial derivatives of Δp=ρgΔh:
u2(Δp)≃(gΔh)2u2(ρ)+(ρΔh)2u2(g)+(ρg)2u2(Δh).
(8)
This displays why a finer scale does not remove uncertainty in mass density or gravitational acceleration. A pressure transducer compared against the column needs its own differential-pressure calibration to establish an electrical response.

Water-column wind-tunnel pressure measurement

U-tube differential manometer OurBigBook.com
NASA's Wind Tunnel Experiment Details, slide 27, describes a practical manometer measurement: partially fill a Tygon tube with water and connect its two ends to total pressure and static pressure ports in a wind tunnel. The total pressure connection pushes its liquid meniscus downward; the vertical length difference supplies the pressure difference. The slide predicts increasing separation as the tunnel speed increases. It supplies an apparatus and method, rather than a table of observed readings.[ref]
A control for this practical is to expose both connections to the same atmospheric pressure before the run: settled liquid meniscus heights should agree in a symmetric column. Read each liquid meniscus at eye level, reconnect sealed tubing to the identified ports, and wait for settling. Recheck the equal-pressure zero afterwards; reverse connections to check the sign. These checks establish neither mass density nor ruler accuracy.[ref]
The inference is a differential pressure from hydrostatic pressure, with stagnation pressure on one side and static pressure on the other in NASA's practical. Converting that difference to a flow speed additionally needs the hypotheses discussed under dynamic pressure and Pitot-static tube. A changing pressure can leave the column oscillating; leaks, blocked pressure tappings or trapped liquid in a gas connection can alter or delay the readout. The column should be read after settling, and temperature should be recorded when choosing the measuring liquid's mass density.
Two corrections clarify the limits. If both gas ports are at the same height and carry the same gas of constant mass density ρg​, keeping its hydrostatic pressure gives pL​−pR​=(ρ−ρg​)gΔh. Different port heights require their separate gas column heights. Also, a curved liquid meniscus can sustain a capillary pressure jump through surface tension. Write JL​,JR​ for liquid pressure minus gas pressure at the two surfaces. Neglecting gas weight, the balance becomes pL​−pR​=ρgΔh+JR​−JL​. Identical meniscus shapes in matching clean bores cancel those jumps; unequal bores or different wetting conditions need not. Thus the useful simplicity of ρgΔh rests on identifiable physical conditions.

Airfoil

Words: 621 Articles: 3
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
An airfoil (British spelling: aerofoil) is the cross-sectional profile of a lifting surface, such as a wing or blade. Its chord is the straight segment from leading edge to trailing edge, with length c; its mean camber line runs midway between its upper and lower surfaces, and its thickness measures their separation. Camber is the departure of that mean line from the chord. The angle of attack describes the profile's orientation relative to the incoming flow. These independent choices let a designer alter the distribution of pressure, lift and drag, rather than simply enlarging the surface. [ref]
The distinction between an airfoil and a finite wing matters. A two-dimensional section model assumes no variation along span and predicts lift per unit span L′. A wing of span b has a spanwise distribution L′(z) and total lift L=∫−b/2b/2​L′(z)dz. Its tip flow and trailing vortices generate a downward induced velocity, called downwash, which changes the local flow seen by the sections. Thus one cannot generally multiply the isolated two-dimensional L′ by b. The wing aspect ratio b2/S measures its span relative to its reference area and helps characterize these three-dimensional effects. [ref]
For a thin section with small camber slopes and small angle of attack, thin airfoil theory predicts
cl​≃2π(α−αL=0​),dαdcl​​≃2π,
(9)
where both angles are in radians and αL=0​ is the zero-lift angle of attack. The model assumes two-dimensional, steady flow, incompressible flow, inviscid flow, an attached outer flow, and smooth departure at a sharp trailing edge (the Kutta condition). This last condition selects the circulation used by the Kutta–Joukowski theorem; with counterclockwise circulation Γ positive and U∞​=U∞​ex​, that theorem gives L′=−ρ∞​U∞​Γ for positive lift towards +ey​. The beauty is that a detailed velocity field collapses to a simple force law, while the geometry enters through αL=0​. [ref] [ref]
A symmetric airfoil has αL=0​=0 in this model: at α=4∘=π/45 the predicted lift coefficient is cl​≃0.439, and reversing α reverses lift. A stipulated cambered section with αL=0​=−2∘ instead predicts cl​≃0.219 at zero angle of attack. These are ideal calculations, not measurements or guarantees for a particular profile. Air parcels on the upper and lower surfaces have no obligation to arrive together at the trailing edge; the pressure and velocity field must satisfy the flow problem. A symmetric lifting section already makes an unequal-path-length explanation inadequate. [ref]
Real airfoils have a viscous boundary layer, even when inviscid flow approximates the outer motion. At sufficiently demanding incidence, flow separation can become extensive and the lift coefficient departs from its approximately linear law, reaches a maximum and may fall: this is aerodynamic stall. Lift does not generally vanish at aerodynamic stall. The onset depends on profile, Reynolds number, surface condition and motion history; 2π(α−αL=0​) predicts neither a universal stall angle nor post-stall behavior. The pressure/balance experiment in lift makes this limit observable by measuring changes in the surface pressure distribution alongside the total force. [ref]

A fluid is a material that flows under sustained shear stress and cannot maintain a static shear stress in its fluid state. Liquids and gases are the usual examples. A Newtonian fluid has deviatoric stress proportional to its rate-of-strain tensor, whereas more general fluid constitutive equations can be nonlinear or have memory. In a porous medium, the fluid occupies connected voids within a load-bearing solid framework. The important distinction is the response to a continuing tangential force: an ordinary elastic solid can settle into a fixed deformation, while an ordinary fluid continues to deform. A fluid can nevertheless be at rest when no unbalanced shear stress drives it. [ref]
For a worked example, place a Newtonian fluid between parallel plates separated by h=1mm, keep the lower plate fixed and move the upper one at U=0.10ms−1. With no-slip boundary conditions, steady flow, no imposed pressure gradient and negligible edge effects, Couette flow has u(y)=Uy/h. For dynamic viscosity μ=0.001Pas, the shear stress magnitude is
τ=μdydu​=μhU​=0.10Pa.
(10)
The velocity gradient describes neighbouring layers sliding at different speeds. Doubling U doubles the required shear stress; maintaining the same velocity keeps producing deformation, rather than fixing a final shape. This gives viscosity a concrete meaning: resistance to a rate of motion, not a prohibition on motion.

A pathline records the motion of one identified fluid element: keep its starting position a and starting time t0​ fixed, and let physical time t advance. In a velocity field u(x,t) its Lagrangian trajectory X(t;t0​,a) solves the initial value problem
dtdX​=u(X(t),t),X(t0​;t0​,a)=a.
(11)
A streamline instead freezes the time argument of the velocity field; a streakline fixes the observation time and varies the release time of many fluid elements. A pathline is useful for answering where a particular parcel goes and how long it takes, rather than merely which way the fluid is moving now. [ref]
For a concrete analytical model, take spatial coordinates x,y in metres, time t≥0 in seconds, and the spatially uniform but time-dependent velocity field
u(x,y,t)=(U,at),U=1 ms−1,a=1 ms−2.
(12)
Its numerical components in these units are (1,t). A fluid element starting at the origin at t0​=0 has the pathline
x(t)=Ut,y(t)=2at2​,y=2U2a​x2.
(13)
At t=1 s it is at (1,0.5) m; at t=2 s it is at (2,2) m. The parabola records earlier, shallower velocity directions as well as the final direction. Differentiating gives (x˙,y˙​)=(U,at) and acceleration (0,a), so this curved pathline needs no spatial variation of the velocity field. More generally the chain rule along a pathline gives df(X(t),t)/dt=∂t​f+u⋅∇f, the material derivative of a transported scalar field.
A motivating tracer demonstration appears in S. J. Kline's film notes: water passes through a contracting channel, and hydrogen bubbles mark a small element at a wire at time t0​. The illustrated element is shown again 4.7 s later, with its accumulated pathline superposed. Following that same marked element across successive film frames records a history; the entire bubble pattern in one frame has a different meaning. [ref]
For a modern version of the readout, use sparse small markers in a transparent water channel, illuminate the viewed plane, and keep an optical camera fixed with a ruler in that plane. Record timestamps and track the same isolated marker between frames; successive positions estimate its pathline and [X(t+Δt)−X(t)]/Δt estimates its velocity. A long exposure records a pathline segment but loses the timing within it, so its total length divided by exposure time gives only mean speed. These are proposed measurement steps based on Jean Hertzberg's teaching guidance, rather than additional measurements from Kline's film. Markers leaving the viewed plane, overlapping tracks and perspective can break particle identification; repeat with a thinner viewed slice and a lower marker concentration. [ref]

The Navier slip boundary condition allows a fluid to slide tangentially past a solid wall while resisting that motion through wall friction in the Navier slip boundary condition. For parallel flow past a flat, impermeable wall translating uniformly with tangential velocity Uw​, write the fluid's tangential velocity as u and its relative tangential velocity as urel​=u−Uw​. Then
urel​=b∂n​u,b≥0,
(14)
where b is the slip length, also written ℓs​. The unit normal n points from the wall into the fluid, and ∂n​u=n⋅∇u is the normal derivative. The separate no-penetration boundary condition requires (u−Uw​)⋅n=0: tangential sliding does not allow flow through the wall.
The sign convention matters. In a channel 0<z<H, the lower wall has inward unit normal +ez​ and the upper wall has inward unit normal −ez​. If both walls obey the Navier slip boundary condition, their tangential velocities satisfy
u(0)−U0​=b0​u′(0),u(H)−UH​=−bH​u′(H).
(15)
Here the prime means the derivative with respect to z. Using +bH​u′(H) at the upper wall would reverse the friction law. The examples Couette flow with a slipping lower wall and planar Poiseuille flow with equal wall slip use different upper-wall boundary conditions.
This flat-wall formula is a local linear model. On a curved wall the Newtonian fluid stress tensor must supply the tangential traction; the normal derivative alone generally misses curvature terms. The author-written review by Lauga, Brenner and Stone states the full strain-based condition with the unit normal directed into the liquid. [ref]
The same review credits Navier's 1823 treatise with the linear slip law. Its history is a reminder that the no-slip boundary condition is an experimentally successful model, whose validity depends on the interface and scale. The history here follows that review rather than a new reading of Navier's original memoir. [ref]

The slip length measures tangential wall mobility in the Navier slip boundary condition. Where the wall shear rate is nonzero,
b=∂n​uurel​​.
(16)
The numerator is a velocity and the denominator has units s−1, so b has units of length. Geometrically, take a local inward normal coordinate s, with the wall at s=0. The tangent line to the relative velocity profile is
urel,lin​(s)=urel​(0)+s∂n​u(0)=(b+s)∂n​u(0).
(17)
It reaches zero at s=−b, a fictitious distance b inside the solid. This extrapolation does not assert that fluid exists there. At a moving wall, extrapolate to the wall's velocity, rather than to zero laboratory velocity. If both the wall shear rate and relative velocity vanish, their ratio cannot determine b.
The useful comparison is b/H, where H is the channel gap. A small absolute slip length can noticeably change volumetric flow rate in a micrometre-scale channel. Measured effective slip length may summarize unresolved interfacial structure; it need not mean literal molecular sliding at every point. The review distinguishes intrinsic, apparent and effective slip and discusses how surface conditions affect measurements. [ref]

Couette flow with a slipping lower wall (u(z)=U(z+b)/(H+b))

Words: 262
Slip length OurBigBook.com
Consider steady flow of a Newtonian fluid in incompressible flow with constant dynamic viscosity μ>0 between parallel plates at z=0 and z=H. The bottom plate is stationary and obeys the Navier slip boundary condition with slip length b. The top plate moves at velocity U>0 and obeys the no-slip boundary condition. There is no streamwise pressure gradient or body force. The Couette flow solution is
u(z)=UH+bz+b​,u(0)=H+bUb​,τ=μu′(z)=H+bμU​.
(18)
Here τ is the constant shear stress magnitude. The lower wall's Navier slip boundary condition holds exactly because bu′(0)=bU/(H+b)=u(0). At the top, u(H)=U is exactly the prescribed no-slip boundary condition; no finite upper-wall slip length is imposed in this example.
For a numerical example, stipulate H=10μm, b=2μm, U=1mms−1 and μ=10−3Pas. The bottom velocity is 0.167mms−1 and the shear stress is 0.0833Pa, compared with 0.100Pa when both plates obey the no-slip boundary condition. The extrapolated profile reaches zero at z=−2μm.
For fixed H, U and μ, b→0 recovers u=Uz/H. As b→∞, u→U throughout the gap and τ→0: the moving upper wall selects the limiting uniform velocity, while the lower wall approaches a stress-free boundary condition. The dynamic viscosity stays positive; the disappearing shear stress comes from the disappearing velocity gradient.
A short derivation uses unidirectional flow: the convective acceleration vanishes and the Navier-Stokes equation reduces to μu′′=0. Write u=Az+B. The bottom condition gives B=bA and the top condition gives A(H+b)=U.

Now both plates at z=0 and z=H are stationary and both obey the Navier slip boundary condition with the same slip length b. (19)
The full volumetric flow rate for channel width W is Q=Wq when side-wall effects are negligible. Thus q has units m2s−1, while Q has units m3s−1. Denote the value at b=0 by q0​=GH3/(12μ).
The two wall checks expose the normal signs:
u′(z)=2μG​(H−2z),u(0)=u(H)=2μGbH​,
(20)
bu′(0)=2μGbH​=u(0),−bu′(H)=2μGbH​=u(H).
(21)
Both Navier slip boundary conditions therefore hold exactly. The two walls exert backward tangential tractions of magnitude GH/2 on the fluid. Increasing b at fixed G adds a uniform velocity offset, leaving the velocity gradient and wall shear stress unchanged. This differs from Couette flow with a slipping lower wall, where upper-wall velocity is fixed and shear stress decreases.
For H=10μm, b=2μm, G=103Pam−1 and μ=10−3Pas, the wall velocity is 10μms−1, the centre velocity is 22.5μms−1, and q=1.83×10−10m2s−1. The enhancement is q/q0​=2.2. Equivalently, a prescribed volumetric flow rate needs only 1/2.2 of the original pressure gradient. This makes slip length useful for estimating pumping requirements in small channels.
At fixed H, G>0 and μ, b→0 recovers ordinary planar Poiseuille flow. As b→∞, the velocity and q grow without bound in this model, although the varying part of the profile stays the same. At exactly zero tangential wall traction, no steady solution can balance this nonzero pressure gradient: u′(0)=u′(H)=0 conflicts with μ[u′(H)−u′(0)]=−GH. Unlimited enhancement is consequently not a prediction for a real channel; finite wall friction, finite driving capacity and the validity of the assumed steady flow must be assessed. At fixed finite q instead, G→0 and the profile approaches uniform velocity q/H.
A short derivation integrates the reduced Navier-Stokes equation μu′′=−G twice. Equal slip lengths and the opposite inward unit normals give u=G[z(H−z)+bH]/(2μ). Its integral over the gap supplies the enhancement factor 1+6b/H.

Buoyancy (Fb​)

Words: 2k Articles: 13
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
Buoyancy is the resultant upward force exerted by a resting fluid on an immersed body in a downward gravitational field. The fluid pushes inward, perpendicular to each part of the body's surface. Because hydrostatic pressure increases with depth, the upward push from below exceeds the downward push from above. Opposite horizontal forces cancel; buoyancy is the remaining vertical force. A sinking body still receives this upward support. [ref]
More precisely, pressure p on a small surface of area dA with outward unit normal vector n exerts
dF=−pndA.
(26)
The minus sign says the force points into the body. On a cube, the top force points down, the bottom force points up, and the side forces cancel in pairs because opposite sides have the same pressure at each depth. This is a surface traction; gravity on the body itself is a separate body force. [ref]
For a computed example, stipulate resting water with constant mass density ρf​=1000 kgm−3 and uniform gravitational acceleration g=9.81 ms−2. A fully immersed cube has side L=0.10 m, top depth ht​=0.20 m and bottom depth hb​=0.30 m. Each horizontal face has area A=L2=0.010 m2, and its volume is V=L3=0.001 m3. Its top and bottom gauge pressures are
pg,t​=ρf​ght​=1962 Pa,pg,b​=ρf​ghb​=2943 Pa.
(27)
The corresponding forces relative to the common surface pressure are pg,t​A=19.62 N downward and pg,b​A=29.43 N upward. Therefore the net buoyancy is
Fb​=(pg,b​−pg,t​)A=9.81 N.
(28)
Using absolute pressures adds the same psurface​A to both face forces, leaving their difference unchanged. Zero gauge pressure at the surface does not mean zero absolute pressure. Increasing both depths by the same amount also leaves buoyancy unchanged in this constant-mass density model.
Archimedes' principle turns this calculation into a rule for bodies of any shape. It explains floating equilibrium and lets us infer an immersed body's volume from the difference between its force from gravity and the force needed to support it. In particular, buoyancy depends on the displaced volume and the surrounding mass density, whereas the body's own mass density decides how its force from gravity compares with that support.

Words: 786 Articles: 3
Buoyancy OurBigBook.com
Archimedes' principle states that buoyancy equals the downward gravitational weight, or weight, of the displaced fluid. In a resting fluid of constant mass density ρf​ under uniform gravitational acceleration g, its magnitude is
Fb​=ρf​gVdisplaced​.
(29)

A short proof outline for a fully immersed body is to imagine replacing it by exactly the fluid it displaces. The surrounding hydrostatic pressure is unchanged. That replacement fluid is at rest, so its upward pressure force must balance its downward force from gravity. The original body receives the same inward pressure forces on the same closed surface, hence the same upward buoyancy.
Equivalently, let Ω be the displaced region, ∂Ω its closed surface and ez​ the upward unit direction. The divergence theorem, applied component by component to the surface integral, and hydrostatic pressure give

(30)
This also explains why horizontal forces cancel even for an irregular shape. A spatially constant surface pressure contributes zero to the closed-surface integral. If the mass density varies with depth, replace ρf​Vdisplaced​ by the mass ∫Ω​ρf​dV of the displaced fluid.
The closed-surface argument assumes that the fluid applies pressure over the entire boundary of a fully immersed body. A body sealing against a tank bottom may have no fluid beneath it; then the lower-face pressure force used in the proof is absent, and a supporting contact force must be treated separately. For partial immersion, the usual buoyancy formula assumes the exposed surface receives the common atmospheric pressure, neglects the much smaller buoyancy from the air, and neglects surface tension.
For the 0.10 m cube in the stipulated water, full immersion displaces 0.001 m3, so Fb​=1000×9.81×0.001=9.81 N. If its uniform mass density is 600 kgm−3, its mass is m=600×0.001=0.600 kg and its downward force from gravity is mg=5.886 N. To hold it fully immersed at rest requires an additional downward force
Fhold​=Fb​−mg=9.81−5.886=3.924 N.
(31)
On release from rest it initially moves upward; its eventual floating equilibrium has a smaller displaced volume. A same-size cube of uniform mass density 1200 kgm−3 has mass 1.200 kg and downward force from gravity 11.772 N. Full immersion still gives 9.81 N of buoyancy, leaving an initial net downward force of 11.772−9.81=1.962 N. Subsequent motion also involves drag.

Torricelli's law (v=2gh​)

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
An ideal fluid issuing from a small hole a vertical depth h below a free surface has speed
v=2gh​.
(37)
Here h is the vertical distance from the free surface to the centre of the orifice, and g is the positive magnitude of gravitational acceleration. The ideal prediction assumes incompressible flow, the same ambient pressure at the free surface and emerging jet, negligible velocity of the reservoir's free surface, and negligible viscous dissipation and surface tension effects. For a falling free surface, a quasi-steady approximation additionally assumes that the local outflow adjusts much faster than h changes. It applies the Bernoulli equation at each instant, rather than claiming that the whole drainage is steady flow.[ref]
A short proof uses a streamline connecting the reservoir's free surface at elevation zs​ to the emerging jet at elevation zo​. With constant mass density ρ, negligible surface speed and no mechanical energy losses, the Bernoulli equation gives
ρpambient​​+gzs​=ρpambient​​+2v2​+gzo​,h=zs​−zo​.
(38)
Equal pressures cancel, leaving v2/2=gh: a unit mass gains the same kinetic energy as a body in free fall through height h. This makes Torricelli's law a useful first estimate before the detailed velocity field is known. At one quarter of the original head, ideal jet speed is one half as large; it is not proportional to head.
Far from the accelerating outlet region, the reservoir has approximately hydrostatic pressure pambient​+ρgh at the outlet's elevation. The emerging jet instead has approximately ambient pressure when surface tension is negligible. Do not assign that bulk hydrostatic pressure to the emerging jet as well as adding the height difference: that would count the available mechanical energy twice. A sealed reservoir, a submerged outlet or significant surface tension changes the pressure conditions and requires a different balance.
Actual volumetric flow rate is commonly represented by a discharge coefficient:
Q=Cd​a2gh​,Cd​=a2gh​Q​,
(39)
where a is the geometric area of the orifice. This definition compares volumetric flow rates, not just speeds. If a nearly uniform jet at its vena contracta has area aj​ and speed vj​, define the two separate ratios Cc​=aj​/a and Cv​=vj​/2gh​. Then Q=aj​vj​ gives Cd​=Cc​Cv​. A contracted jet can consequently have a speed close to 2gh​ while Cd​ is appreciably below one. No particular Cd​ is universal: calibrate it for the opening and operating range.

Tap water filled a semitransparent polypropylene beaker with a marked volume scale and drilled side openings. Some trials added horizontal outlet tubes. Temperature was measured, and dye checked that the water had settled before uncovering the outlet. The readout was elapsed time at successive volume marks. Outlet tubes introduced viscosity effects. This experiment tests a useful operating range, rather than proving ideal drainage down to zero head.[ref]

The drag coefficient measures a drag force against a specified scale of force. Let U=vbody​−u∞​ be the body's velocity relative to the distant, undisturbed fluid, and let U=∣U∣>0 be its relative speed. For fluid density ρ, drag force magnitude FD​ and reference area A>0, define

For a sphere of radius a, the usual choice is the frontal area A=πa2. Choosing its entire surface area 4πa2 instead divides the reported drag coefficient by four for the same physical drag force. Comparing coefficients without comparing their reference areas can therefore be misleading. [ref]

(50)
Thus the drag coefficient is neither necessarily constant nor bounded above by one. The formula containing U2 still describes linear drag here, because the drag coefficient varies as 1/U. The relation CD​=24/Red​ is the leading small-Reynolds number approximation, not a measured curve valid at every Reynolds number. [ref]
For a worked example, stipulate dynamic viscosity μ=0.10Pas, density ρ=1000kgm−3, radius a=10−4m and relative speed U=10−3ms−1. Within the stated Stokes drag law assumptions,
Red​=0.002,CD​=12000,FD​=6π×10−8N≈1.88495559×10−7N.
(51)
Doubling the relative speed with all other parameters fixed gives Red​=0.004 and CD​=6000: the predicted drag force doubles to 3.76991118×10−7N. Falsely holding the drag coefficient at 12000 would instead quadruple the drag force. Both particle Reynolds numbers remain small, so the comparison is within the creeping-flow approximation.
The useful idea is to separate the force scale from the dependence on geometry and flow conditions. A drag coefficient can help compare experiments, but changing Reynolds number can change the coefficient itself; NASA Glenn explicitly stresses matching the relevant flow conditions. The elegant cancellation above also exposes a common mistake: a drag coefficient definition does not by itself impose a quadratic drag law.

Words: 597 Articles: 4
Drag (physics) OurBigBook.com
Quadratic drag has magnitude proportional to the square of the relative speed and points opposite to the relative velocity.

Here density ρ, reference area A and drag coefficient CD​ are held fixed over the modeled range of relative speeds. The vector formula makes the direction explicit: the drag force on the body opposes its motion relative to the fluid, and vanishes at U=0. For a general body, orientation and other flow conditions can affect the drag coefficient; treating it as a constant requires a regime in which that is an adequate approximation. [ref]
Compare two distinct models at a chosen relative speed U0​>0. A linear drag model has FD​(U)/FD​(U0​)=U/U0​, while a constant-coefficient quadratic drag model has FD​(U)/FD​(U0​)=(U/U0​)2. At U=2U0​ their drag force ratios are two and four respectively.
This distinction matters when estimating terminal velocity or trajectories such as descent from rest under quadratic drag: doubling relative speed increases the resistance much more strongly in the quadratic drag model. An approximately constant drag coefficient can occur in another Reynolds number regime; its use must be justified there. Conversely, substituting the creeping-flow sphere coefficient CD​=24/Red​ into FD​=21​ρU2ACD​ recovers linear drag, so writing this general formula does not make the resistance quadratic. Neither approximation should be extended across all Reynolds numbers.
The distinction already appears in the original investigation underlying the Stokes drag law, read on 9 December 1850: article 42 identifies resistance proportional to relative speed and distinguishes it from a contribution proportional to the square of relative speed. [ref]

(53)
Here s is an auxiliary curve parameter, with units of seconds in this convention; advancing s does not advance physical time. Any regular reparameterization preserves the tangent geometry. Where ux​=0, a planar streamline satisfies dy/dx=uy​/ux​ evaluated at time T. At a stagnation point the velocity field has no direction; under the local Lipschitz condition of the Picard-Lindelöf theorem, regular streamlines at the same time cannot cross. A streamline answers which directions fit together now, making it useful for describing local flow geometry. [ref]
In the analytical velocity field (U,at) introduced under pathline, the streamline through the origin at time T is
y=UaT​x.
(54)

Its instantaneous streamline at the final position (2,2) m is instead y−2 m=2(x−2 m): the pathline is tangent to that streamline at its current endpoint, although its recorded history does not lie along it.
The green streamline uses the velocity field at T=2 s throughout; the orange pathline uses times 0≤t≤2 s; the purple streakline uses different release times at the single observation time T=2 s. The grey arrows all show the instantaneous velocity direction at T. These are exact analytical curves with chosen units, not measured dye shapes.
In a steady flow in a fixed reference frame, a pathline and a streamline solve the same autonomous ordinary differential equation. Uniqueness makes each particle released from a fixed point follow the same integral curve, so its pathline, the streakline from that point and the streamline share one geometrical curve. Finite recording or release intervals usually show different segments of that curve; the comparison assumes particles stay in the domain and treats stationary fluid elements separately. Neither two-dimensionality nor incompressibility is needed for this coincidence. Steadiness is sufficient, but is not necessary: u(x,t)=g(t)v(x) with smooth g(t)>0 changes speed while preserving the same integral curves. In a general time-dependent velocity field, however, the three curves differ. Kline explains why continuous dye release in steady flow can therefore display streamlines. [ref]
For two-dimensional incompressible flow, the convention u=(∂y​ψ,−∂x​ψ) gives u⋅∇ψ=0, so regular streamlines are level sets of the stream function at each frozen time. In time-dependent incompressible flow, that does not force a pathline to stay on one numerical value of ψ: its material derivative is Dψ/Dt=∂t​ψ. The distinction is the difference between a geometric snapshot and a parcel's history.

Incompressible flow (∇⋅u=0)

Words: 458 Articles: 4
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
An incompressible flow preserves the volume of each moving fluid element. Its local condition is zero velocity divergence, ∇⋅u=0. Combined with mass conservation, it says that each parcel's mass density stays unchanged as it moves. This does not require every parcel to have the same mass density: an initially nonuniform distribution can be transported without compression. Nor does incompressibility require a constant velocity or constant pressure.
For positive mass density, the continuity equation makes the equivalence precise:
∂t∂ρ​+∇⋅(ρu)=0,DtDρ​+ρ∇⋅u=0,DtD​=∂t∂​+u⋅∇.
(83)
The material derivative follows a fluid element. Thus Dρ/Dt=0 if and only if the velocity field is a divergence-free vector field. The distinction between following a parcel and observing a fixed position prevents confusing incompressibility with an unchanging density field. [ref]
For a rigid pipe with impermeable walls, no leaks and steady flow, mass conservation at constant mass density implies a constant volumetric flow rate:
Q=∫A​u⋅ndA=AU,A1​U1​=A2​U2​.
(84)
Here n points downstream, A is the section's area and U is the mean normal velocity, not necessarily the centreline speed. No assumption of inviscid flow or a uniform velocity profile is needed. If unequal amounts entered and left a fixed segment, its mass would accumulate, contradicting steady flow.
For a worked example, take horizontal water flow with stipulated mass density 1000kgm−3, inlet radius R1​=0.010m, outlet radius R2​=0.005m and inlet mean velocity U1​=0.20ms−1. The circular areas give
Q=πR12​U1​=2π×10−5m3s−1,U2​=πR22​Q​=0.80ms−1.
(85)
The radius halves, the area falls to one quarter, and the mean velocity quadruples. The mass flow rate is ρQ=0.02πkgs−1. The same amount of water passes both sections each second; narrowing changes its speed rather than compressing it. The Reynolds number and Bernoulli's principle discussions use this same example to examine viscous effects and the additional assumptions needed to calculate pressure.

A streakline at observation time T is the set of present positions of all fluid elements that passed through one fixed release point a during a specified history of injection. For continuous release over τ0​≤τ≤T, solve a different initial value problem for each release time τ:
∂t∂X​(t;τ,a)=u(X(t;τ,a),t),X(τ;τ,a)=a,ST​={X(T;τ,a):τ0​≤τ≤T}.
(86)
Thus a pathline varies t for one particle; a streakline varies τ while holding T fixed. Interrupted release gives only the corresponding subsets of the streakline. A moving nozzle requires a time-dependent release position instead, so the standard fixed-point definition should not silently be applied to it. Continuous release makes streaklines easy to observe and useful for showing where material from one source has reached. [ref]
In the analytical velocity field (U,at) of pathline, a particle released at the origin at time τ follows
x(t;τ)=U(t−τ),y(t;τ)=2a​(t2−τ2),t≥τ.
(87)
Observe all particles together at time T, after continuous release from τ=0:
x=U(T−τ),y=2a​(T2−τ2),y=UaT​x−2U2a​x2,0≤x≤UT.
(88)
For U=1 ms−1, a=1 ms−2 and T=2 s, the streakline is the downward-curving parabola y=2x−x2/2 in metre coordinates. Releases at τ=0,1,2 s occupy (2,2), (1,1.5) and (0,0) m, respectively. At x=1 m, the streakline lies above the pathline y=x2/2 and below the origin's streamline y=2x. All particles nevertheless have the same present velocity (1,2) ms−1. The streakline slope dy/dx=aτ/U generally differs from the present velocity slope aT/U; they agree at the nozzle. The oldest particle is the downstream endpoint, which explains why the pathline and streakline meet there without being the same curve.
Each panel fixes one observation time. Coloured dots are the present positions of particles with the indicated release times; dashed pathlines show those particles' earlier histories. The black streakline connects present positions of the continuously released family, including release times between the sampled dots. After T=1 s, particles already present keep moving and new ones enter at the origin, so the later streakline is not a frozen record of the earlier one. Injection beginning only at τ=1 s would show just 0≤x≤1 m of the T=2 s curve. Both panels are diffusion-free analytical models, not experimental photographs.
Kline's contracting-channel demonstration switches from marking an element to continuous bubble production at a marking wire: the resulting trace is a streakline. The apparatus therefore changes the curve being displayed by changing the marking history, even with the same channel. A wire produces a family of traces; conceptually each fixed emitting location supplies its own streakline. Individual bubbles are markers rather than perfect fluid elements: Jean Hertzberg's teaching notes describe hydrogen production by electrolysis at a thin cathode wire and warn that larger bubbles have more buoyancy. [ref] [ref]
A dye version uses a small fixed injection port upstream in a transparent water channel, a dilute premix of dye with the channel water, illumination and a fixed optical camera. Start continuous injection at a recorded time τ0​ and take a short exposure at T: the visible filament approximates a streakline, not the accumulated pathline of one particle. Repeat with the same port and imaging geometry after changing the flow with time; compare the filament against local directions estimated from short displacements of sparse markers at T. Agreement in a steady flow and possible disagreement when the flow changes are the predictions being tested; no measured curves are claimed here. The protocol follows Hertzberg's advice to use small ports, little injected volume and a dilute premix with matched density and viscosity. Check for nozzle disturbance by reducing injection rate, for buoyancy by watching the premix in still water, and for diffusion by comparing filament widths at different ages. Keep exposure short enough to suppress motion blur. Dye concentration approximates a passive scalar only when it has negligible feedback on the velocity field; finite port width, diffusion and out-of-plane motion limit how literally a visible filament can be read as a geometrical streakline. [ref]

At steady state, the displacement-ventilation interface lies where the total plume volume flux equals the imposed ventilation flux. For one triangular-profile wall line plume with kinematic buoyancy flux B0​, entrainment coefficient α, and ventilation flux A per unit span,
h=(3α2​)2/3B01/3​A​.
(104)

Single-opening exchange flow

Words: 65 Articles: 1
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
A tall opening between fluids of different densities can support simultaneous inflow below a neutral pressure level and outflow above it. For a symmetric opening with a Boussinesq hydrostatic pressure difference and equal discharge coefficients, the neutral level lies at mid-height.

Neutral pressure level

Words: 24
Single-opening exchange flow OurBigBook.com
The neutral pressure level is the height at which indoor and outdoor hydrostatic pressures agree. Flow through an opening reverses direction across this level.

Stratified-room plume-exchange model

Words: 36
Natural ventilation OurBigBook.com
A stratified-room plume-exchange model balances the upward volume transported by a warm plume against downward transport by cold wall plumes. A global buoyancy balance relates the source flux to the buoyancy carried out through the vents.

Homologous spherical flow (u=q(t)r)

Words: 44 Articles: 1
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A homologous spherical flow has velocity proportional to radius. Its velocity gradient is q(t)I and its velocity divergence is 3q(t).

Self-similar ansatz

Words: 27
Homologous spherical flow OurBigBook.com
A self-similar ansatz expresses evolving fields through a dimensionless similarity coordinate such as x=r/R(t), reducing a partial differential equation to ordinary differential equations in x.

Orifice

Words: 37 Articles: 1
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
An orifice is a small opening through which a fluid can flow.

Vena contracta

Words: 27
Orifice OurBigBook.com
The vena contracta is the narrowest jet section after an opening. Its area may be smaller than the opening area, so the jet speed and volumetric flow rate require separate comparisons with ideal flow.

Nozzle

Words: 293 Articles: 6
Fluid mechanics OurBigBook.com
A nozzle shapes a passage to control the speed and direction of a fluid flow. In compressible flow, converging-diverging passages can accelerate a gas through a sonic flow throat into supersonic flow.

Isentropic nozzle flow

Words: 268 Articles: 5
Nozzle OurBigBook.com
Smooth adiabatic nozzle flow without entropy production. In a steady quasi-one-dimensional ideal-gas model, ρuA and u2/2+cp​T are constant along the passage. A converging-diverging passage can connect subsonic and supersonic branches through a sonic throat when reservoir and back-pressure conditions select that branch.

Adiabatic nozzle terminal speed (u∞​=c∗​(γ+1)/(γ−1)​)

Words: 55
Isentropic nozzle flow OurBigBook.com
For a lossless polytropic flow with γ>1, negligible gravity and a sonic throat, the Bernoulli function is u2/2+cs2​/(γ−1)=(γ+1)c∗2​/[2(γ−1)]. On an expanding supersonic branch for which ρ→0, the specific enthalpy vanishes and the limiting velocity is the displayed value. If area grows as Cr2, mass conservation further gives ρ∼M˙/(Cu∞​r2). A subsonic pressure-confined branch need not have this asymptotic behavior.

Sonic density of a polytropic nozzle (ρ∗​=[M˙/(A∗​γK​)]2/(γ+1))

Words: 44
Isentropic nozzle flow OurBigBook.com
For steady polytropic flow with p=Kργ, K>0, γ>1, a sonic section has u∗​=c∗​=(γKρ∗γ−1​)1/2. Substitution in mass conservation M˙=A∗​ρ∗​u∗​ gives the displayed density. These conditions fix the sonic state for a prescribed flux and throat area, subject to compatible reservoir and downstream boundary conditions.

de Laval nozzle

Words: 42
Isentropic nozzle flow OurBigBook.com
A converging-diverging nozzle that can accelerate a compressible flow from subsonic to supersonic speed through a sonic throat. The nozzle area-velocity relation requires acceleration in a converging subsonic section and a diverging supersonic section. Reservoir and downstream pressures determine whether this transonic branch operates; the shape alone does not ensure choked flow.

Nozzle area-Mach number relation (A/A∗​)

Words: 41
Isentropic nozzle flow OurBigBook.com
For a calorically perfect gas on a steady isentropic nozzle branch,
A∗​A​=M1​[γ+12​(1+2γ−1​M2)](γ+1)/(2(γ−1)).
(105)
Here A∗​ is the sonic area. An area ratio greater than one generally admits a subsonic and a supersonic root; boundary conditions choose the physical branch. Numerical inversion must retain that branch information.

Nozzle area-velocity relation (AdA​=(M2−1)udu​)

Words: 45
Isentropic nozzle flow OurBigBook.com
Steady mass conservation, inviscid momentum balance and dp=cs2​dρ give dlnA=(M2−1)dlnu, where M=u/cs​. A smooth sonic crossing needs an area extremum; a minimum-area throat supports an accelerating subsonic-to-supersonic branch. A throat is a necessary geometric condition, not a sufficient specification of operating pressures.
